ledger.sentence: An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the electrical activity of the heart.
ledger.note: BHF/NHS: ECG records the heart's electrical activity; used to check heart rate and rhythm.

ledger.sentence: The British Heart Foundation describes it as a simple test that records the heart's rhythm, its rate and its electrical activity.
ledger.note: BHF: records heart rate/rhythm and electrical activity.

ledger.sentence: Each heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal, and the machine picks these signals up through sensors on the skin.
ledger.note: Heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal; NHS says electrodes on skin record the electrical impulses.

ledger.sentence: The result is a graph of the signals.
ledger.note: An ECG trace is a graph of signals; basic fact, not directly retrieved.

ledger.sentence: Sticky patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest and connected to the machine.
ledger.note: NHS: sticky electrodes on arms, legs and chest, wires to the machine.

ledger.sentence: The British Heart Foundation describes the test as quick and painless.
ledger.note: BHF: test takes a few minutes and is completely painless; NHS 111 Wales wording not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The NHS puts a standard ECG at about 5 minutes.
ledger.note: Whittington page not retrieved; NHS page puts the test at about 5 minutes.

ledger.sentence: People are asked to lie still because movement can affect the recording.
ledger.note: NHS: you lie still because moving can affect the results.

ledger.sentence: The British Heart Foundation says an ECG can help doctors to tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past.
ledger.note: BHF: can help doctors tell if you are having a heart attack or have had one in the past.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says an ECG is usually done when a doctor suspects symptoms of a heart attack, coronary heart disease or an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia).
ledger.note: NHS: usually done if a doctor thinks you may have symptoms of a heart attack, coronary heart disease or an arrhythmia. Cardiomyopathy not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: A standard ECG captures only what happens while it is recording.
ledger.note: NCBI paper: a 12-lead ECG is a short snapshot and can miss paroxysmal arrhythmias. BHF page not confirmed verbatim.

ledger.sentence: A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording.
ledger.note: Source says a snapshot can miss paroxysmal arrhythmias; "only if" is stronger.

ledger.sentence: That is why longer recordings or other heart tests are sometimes arranged.
ledger.note: Holter/ambulatory monitoring is used to detect arrhythmias a 12-lead snapshot misses.

ledger.sentence: An ambulatory ECG, sometimes called Holter monitoring, records the heart's electrical activity continuously while the person goes about daily life.
ledger.note: NHS: portable recorder worn; Leeds: worn all day and night; PMC: Holters are wearable portable ECGs.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says people are usually asked to wear it for 24 to 48 hours, but it can be up to 7 days.
ledger.note: NHS: usually 24 to 48 hours but can be up to 7 days. Attribution to BHF not confirmed.

ledger.sentence: It is used to look for heart rhythm problems that a short recording may miss.
ledger.note: Palpitations and atrial fibrillation not retrieved; general purpose of catching missed rhythms is supported.

ledger.sentence: An exercise ECG monitors the heart while the person exercises and the heart is working harder.
ledger.note: NHS: ECG may be done during exercise; BHF: exercise ECG records heart while walking on treadmill or cycling.

ledger.sentence: The British Heart Foundation describes an exercise ECG as an ECG recorded while the person walks on a treadmill or cycles, used to see how the heart behaves under exertion and to look for coronary heart disease.
ledger.note: BHF: walk or cycle, used to see how the heart behaves under exertion and look for coronary heart disease. Wording about blood through coronary arteries not confirmed.

ledger.sentence: Doctors may suggest it for symptoms such as dizzy spells or blackouts.
ledger.note: BHF mentions dizzy spells or blackouts; chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: It is also used after procedures such as angioplasty, and to help set exercise levels for cardiac rehabilitation.
ledger.note: BHF: may be asked after a procedure such as angioplasty; guides exercise levels in cardiac rehabilitation.

ledger.sentence: The person walks or cycles at a gentle pace that gradually gets harder, and staff watch closely.
ledger.note: BHF: gentle pace, gradually harder, staff watch closely and tell you when to stop. Stopping at any point not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says people may need a follow-up appointment to talk about their ECG results.
ledger.note: Referring doctor receiving report not retrieved for ECG; NHS says a follow-up appointment may be needed.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says ECG results may be available on the same day, but can take a few weeks depending on the type of ECG.
ledger.note: NHS: results may be same day but can take a few weeks depending on ECG type. BHF exercise-ECG wait not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The British Heart Foundation says to call 999 immediately for signs of a heart attack, such as sudden chest pain that does not ease after a few minutes of rest.
ledger.note: Safety instruction with qualifiers (severe, spreading, breathlessness) not matching source. BHF: call 999 for signs of a heart attack, e.g. sudden chest pain that does not ease after a few minutes of rest.

ledger.sentence: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, including its rate and rhythm.
ledger.note: BHF/NHS: records electrical activity, used to check heart rate and rhythm.

ledger.sentence: A standard ECG is quick and painless, and patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest.
ledger.note: BHF: quick, painless; NHS: electrodes on arms, legs and chest.

ledger.sentence: A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording, which is why longer monitoring is sometimes used.
ledger.note: Snapshot can miss paroxysmal arrhythmias; "only if" too strong.

ledger.sentence: An ECG can help doctors tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past.
ledger.note: Heart attack supported; "other tests may be needed" not retrieved.
